title: Sifnos Excursions | Tables, Clay & Footpaths | Suites With Keith
description: What I would actually book on Sifnos: the private cooking, pottery, farm and hiking days, the beaches worth the drive, and the tables I send everyone to, on one map.
sub: The island Greeks go to eat. Here is everything I would actually book, from the kitchen and the potter's wheel to the beaches and the tables.

rules.p: Sifnos is small and slow on purpose. Three nights covers the beaches and the best tables; four leaves room for a hike and a class without a single early alarm.

The two hill villages sit in the middle of everything. Platis Gialos, Vathi, Faros and Kastro are all fifteen to twenty minutes away, and the evening stroll through Apollonia is half the reason to come.

rules.h: Book the tables before the boat
rules.p: There are fewer than a dozen tables on Sifnos I plan around, and in July and August the good ones are gone a week out. Send me those first and the rest can stay loose.

map_intro: No airport, one port, and a mountain spine with the villages strung along the top. Ferries dock at Kamares in the west; Apollonia, Artemonas and Kastro sit in the middle and the east; the beaches fan out to the south. Tap any pin for what it is.

logistics.p: Everything comes in at Kamares. Roughly two and a half hours on the fast boat from Piraeus, or under an hour from Milos and Serifos. There is no airport, which is a big part of why it stays the way it is.
Roads are good and short. A small car or a driver for the stay makes the beaches and the dinners easy; taxis exist but there are only a handful on the island.
Late May through June, and September into early October. Warm water, open tavernas, and none of the August crush on the Kastro lanes.

sections.intro: These are the days I arrange myself, privately for the two of you or your group. Sifnos is the island of Tselementes, the father of the modern Greek cookbook, and it has been turning clay since antiquity, so the classes here are the real thing rather than a show put on for visitors.

cards.h: Cooking class in a village kitchen
cards.p: A morning in a Sifnian home kitchen with a local cook, making the dishes the island is known for: revithada slow-baked in a clay pot, mastelo, and the little pastries for after. Lunch is what you made, with local wine at the table.
cards.verdict: The one I would protect if you only do one thing here.

cards.p: Sifnos has been making pottery for three thousand years and a handful of family workshops still fire in wood kilns by the sea. Time at the wheel with the potter, then your piece glazed, fired and shipped home.
Out to a working farm in the hills for the cheese, honey, capers and thyme Sifnos cooks with. Walk the terraces with the family that runs it, then a long table under the trees with what they make.

The island has some of the best waymarked footpaths in the Cyclades, past dovecotes, chapels and ancient watchtowers. I match the route to how hard you want to work, from the easy coastal walk to Chrysopigi to the climb up to the monastery on Profitis Ilias, and end it at a taverna.

sections.intro: Sifnos beaches are small, sheltered and mostly sandy, with a taverna on almost every one. Choose by mood: a long lazy day on the sand, or a swim off the rocks below a village.

cards.p: The long, easy one. A wide sweep of sand with Omega3, Maiòlica and To Steki along it, so lunch is a few steps from the towel.
A near-enclosed bay with water like a lake and the little Taxiarchis chapel at the water's edge. Tables in the sand at Tsikali for lunch, and the best place on the island to do nothing.
The whitewashed monastery out on its rock, and the small sandy cove right beside it. Swim at Apokofto, walk out to the monastery, and lunch at the taverna above the beach.
A tiny fishing harbor with two little beaches a short walk apart. Fasolou is the quieter one. Pelicanos sits right on the sand at Faros.
No sand, just deep blue water. Seralia is the old harbor below Kastro; Poulati is a ladder into the sea under a cliff-top monastery. Go late afternoon, then walk up to Loggia for sunset.
Cheronissos is a fishing hamlet at the very top of the island, with pottery workshops and a taverna on the bay. Vroulidia, on the way, is a pebble cove with the clearest water on Sifnos.

eat_intro: Sifnos has a better table-to-acre ratio than anywhere in the Cyclades. These are the ones I send everyone to.

items.p: A tiny beachside fish bar with an outsized reputation: ceviche, sashimi and inventive seafood small plates with a Greek-only wine list. Best fish on the island. Reserve ahead; lunch is lovely.

A clifftop natural wine bar above the Church of the Seven Martyrs, with 100+ small-producer Greek wines, cheese boards and vinyl playing. The golden-hour tables are the most coveted seats on Sifnos, so arrive before 7pm.
Cantina's laid-back sister restaurant: tables in the sand, great cocktails and the same seasonal ethos. The perfect swim, then lunch, then linger day. Also books via WhatsApp.
Design-led Mediterranean a few steps from the water. Think raw sea bass with lemon verbena and cured mackerel, all built on local ingredients.
Farm-to-table fine dining in the hotel's own kitchen garden, perched on a cliff over the Aegean. Tasting menu, à la carte, or a tapas-and-cocktails bar menu. This is your dress-up dinner night.
A family-run taverna with tables in the sand under tamarisk trees. They raise their own meat and make their own Sifnian goat cheese. Order the mastelo, the wine-braised goat.
The classic beachfront taverna: grilled octopus, fried calamari and revithada, Sifnos' famous chickpea soup, right on the sand. Easy, and no reservation needed.
A historic kafeneio on Apollonia's main lane: Greek coffee, homemade sweets and meze at an old-world pace. Great for an evening stroll through town when the alleys are buzzing.

eat_outro: Omega3, Loggia's sunset tables and Bostani are the three to lock in before you land. Send me the ones you want and I will hold them.
